claim: Endorsement of traditional masculinity is associated with less favourable attitudes to psychological help-seeking and greater self-stigma.
effect_size: r=-.379 (attitudes); r=+.351 (self-stigma); GRC r=-.211 / +.300
limitations: Correlational; does not test any wording; Global-North-weighted samples
male_specific: Yes (about men only; no cross-gender comparison)

claim: Masculine norms are multidimensional; self-reliance, power over women and playboy norms relate most adversely to mental health and help-seeking, while primacy of work does not.
original_study: Wong et al. conformity to masculine norms meta-analysis
effect_size: Overall unfavourable r<=.19 (<5% shared variance); norm-specific variation
limitations: Small overall effect; correlational; masculinity does not 'cause' mental illness

claim: Average adult sex differences in broad language dimensions (talkativeness, assertiveness, affiliative speech) are small.
limitations: Older literature; contexts aggregated

claim: Everyday talkativeness differences by sex appear only in some life stages and disappear in others.
original_study: Tidwell et al. naturalistic EAR registered report
effect_size: Women aged 25-64 ~3,000 more words/day; no notable gap in younger and older bands
limitations: Binary sex categories; word quantity is not communication style

claim: Roughly 78% of documented psychological gender differences fall in the close-to-zero or small range.
effect_size: 78% of effects d<=0.35; verbal ability near zero
limitations: Cannot capture micro-pragmatic conversational nuance

claim: Men report preferring coded or colloquial everyday language for entering mental-health topics alongside dynamic action/growth framing.
effect_size: Three inductive themes: coded language; masculine metaphor; dynamism/action/growth
direction: Preference for indirect entry + direct action
limitations: Qualitative; no behavioural comparison; preference != effectiveness

claim: Working-class men's masculinities can support rather than only suppress disclosure when help-seeking is integrated into their own construction of responsible manhood.
effect_size: Not quantified
direction: Masculinity can facilitate as well as inhibit
limitations: Qualitative; setting-specific

claim: Male-targeted media campaigns can improve some help-seeking attitudes/beliefs for depression, but suicide-specific campaigns show mixed results and components cannot be isolated.
effect_size: Heterogeneous; generally favourable for depression campaigns
limitations: Heterogeneity; variable quality; wording confounded with imagery/channel/spend

claim: Gender-tailored male suicide-prevention interventions have not shown clear effects on suicide attempts, ideation or depression in randomised evidence.
research_design: Systematic review of RCTs and other designs
effect_size: No clear RCT effect on clinical outcomes; help-seeking mixed; attitudes not clearly improved
limitations: Heterogeneous interventions; moderate-to-high risk of bias

claim: A humour-rich, masculinity-parodying digital intervention did not outperform an active control on suicidal ideation or depression.
predictor_iv: Man Therapy vs active control website
effect_size: Both improved (SI slope -0.23 [-0.29,-0.16]; depression -0.21 [-0.23,-0.18]); NO difference by assignment
limitations: Single US state; multi-component intervention; active comparator also substantial; humour not isolated

claim: Man Therapy participants showed somewhat higher odds of actual professional help-seeking in a secondary analysis.
limitations: Borderline significance; secondary outcome; humour not isolated from screening/resources

claim: Mental-health literacy interventions among athletes improved knowledge, stigma, attitudes and intentions but produced no measurable change in actual help-seeking behaviour.
outcome_dv: Knowledge; stigma; attitude; intention; ACTUAL help-seeking
effect_size: Small-to-medium on proximal outcomes; NULL on behaviour at post and follow-up
limitations: Athlete populations; mixed study quality; not Indonesia

claim: Sports-club affiliation can activate social identity strongly enough to overcome prior reluctance to join health programmes.
original_study: Timm et al. rapid realist review
effect_size: Not pooled; consistent realist mechanism
limitations: Skewed to middle-aged, overweight, predominantly White fans; setting confounded with wording

claim: A football-club-embedded, gender-sensitised programme produced sustained weight loss in men aged 35-65.
population: Overweight/obese men recruited via football clubs
effect_size: -4.9 kg difference, 95% CI ~ -5.9 to -4.0
limitations: Cannot isolate language from setting, facilitator, group, identity or programme design

claim: A peer-delivered workplace suicide-prevention programme improved mental-health literacy and helping intentions; behavioural and stigma effects were weaker.
sample_size: 12 papers; separate review of 12 articles/4 interventions
effect_size: Strongest for literacy and intentions
limitations: Limited high-quality behavioural/suicide evidence; methodological quality mostly not strong

claim: Behaviour-change techniques including relatable male role models, psychoeducation, symptom recognition, active problem-solving, signposting and building on valued male traits appear in more successful male help-seeking interventions.
effect_size: Not pooled (heterogeneity prevented meta-analysis)
limitations: Components coexist; cannot isolate 'strength' or masculinity reframing as active ingredient

claim: Men's Sheds and similar side-by-side activity settings are associated with reduced isolation and improved wellbeing, mainly among older men.
original_study: Men's Sheds systematic and scoping reviews
research_design: Systematic/scoping review of mostly non-randomised evidence
effect_size: Generally promising; heterogeneous measurement
confidence: MODERATE (for model); VERY LOW for the word 'men's'
limitations: Selection effects; older skew; label not isolated; poor generalisation to working-age men

claim: An explicit 'Real Men' branded depression brochure performed no better than an identical gender-neutral brochure; an autonomy-supportive male-sensitive brochure did reduce self-stigma.
original_study: Real Men Real Depression campaign evaluations
population: Depressed adult men not in care
predictor_iv: Masculinity-policing label vs neutral vs autonomy-supportive male-sensitive
effect_size: Real Men = no incremental benefit vs neutral; male-sensitive autonomy format reduced self-stigma
confidence: STRONG (for this rare true wording test)
limitations: Post-exposure intentions rather than clinic visits; US only; ~2006-2010 vintage

claim: Gender-coded wording effects depend on the recipient's gender-role identity, not simply on being male: strongly masculine-identified men uniquely disliked communal wording while other men evaluated both styles positively.
predictor_iv: Agentic vs communal wording x endorser gender
effect_size: No universal male preference for masculine wording; subgroup effect for masculine-identified men
limitations: Not a literal 'for men' label test; survey context limits external validity

claim: Responses to hypermasculine advertising depend on endorsement of specific masculine norms (winning, heterosexual self-presentation, power over women) rather than on being male.
predictor_iv: Masculinity threat; hypermasculine vs neutral ad
effect_size: Norm-specific moderation
limitations: Hypermasculine content differs from a bare demographic label

claim: Experimentally threatening masculine adequacy produces measurable responses, strongest for immediate negative affect and reduced self-perceived masculinity.
confidence: STRONG for genuine threat; NOT applicable to ordinary 'for men' labels
limitations: Heterogeneous; Western/heterosexual samples; distal behavioural effects less secure

claim: The published masculinity-threat literature shows substantial selection for statistical significance, with behavioural outcomes the weakest evidential tier and at least one influential effect failing preregistered replication.
effect_size: Moderate expected replicability; behavioural outcomes weakest
limitations: Does not itself estimate label effects

claim: Freedom-threatening (controlling) language reliably increases anger, negative cognitions and measured reactance, and anger in turn relates negatively to persuasion.
effect_size: r=.21 (anger); r=.17 (negative cognition); r=.20 (reactance); anger-persuasion r=-.23
limitations: NOT masculinity-specific; immediate outcomes only; long-term cumulative effects unknown

claim: Masculine cues can function as identity reassurance where a behaviour or product is already coded feminine, altering men's choices.
original_study: Brough et al. green-feminine stereotype programme
effect_size: Masculine cues reduced gender-incongruity penalty
limitations: Does not show masculine branding helps gender-neutral categories

claim: Men avoid feminine-coded options when the choice is publicly visible, but not when it is private.
original_study: White & Dahl dissociative reference group experiments
predictor_iv: Feminine label x public vs private consumption
effect_size: Public avoidance; private parity; asymmetric (women did not mirror it)
limitations: Student convenience samples; hypothetical choices

claim: Masculine-coded recruitment language reduces applications from women and from weakly gender-identified men without increasing applications from traditional men.
effect_size: Neutral wording expanded the pool without cost
limitations: Recruitment domain; may not transfer to health communication

claim: Masculine framing of a feminine-coded food category reduced perceived femininity but did NOT increase willingness among traditional men; it appealed only to men already endorsing progressive masculinities.
original_study: Scholz et al. plant-based framing experiment
predictor_iv: Masculine lexical framing vs sensory framing
effect_size: Perception shifted; behaviour intention did not (for traditional men)
limitations: Online hypothetical scenario; no behavioural follow-up

claim: A pilot survey found the term 'toxic masculinity' rated substantially more negatively than 'positive' or 'traditional' masculinity, with ideological variation.
effect_size: Substantial dislike of 'toxic masculinity'
limitations: Convenience sample; no randomised wording conditions; participants knew they were rating terminology

claim: In an anti-violence education trial roughly 20% of boys resisted when 'toxic masculinity' framing presented men primarily as collective perpetrators; researchers advised abandoning the term in intervention.
original_study: Haslop et al. classroom intervention study
effect_size: ~20% overt resistance; verbatim: 'it kind of showed men as all monsters'
limitations: Educational workshop setting; adolescents not adults; qualitative

claim: A nationally representative latent profile analysis found the large majority of adult men in low-hostility profiles; only about one in ten fell into a high-centrality traditionalist cluster.
original_study: Hill, Barlow et al. latent profile analysis
predictor_iv: Gender centrality; sexism; SDO; attitudes to gender initiatives
effect_size: 35.4% egalitarian; 53.8% pragmatic moderates; 10.8% traditionalists
direction: Most men are not the stereotype
limitations: Single country; self-report; profile labels are analytic conveniences

claim: Precarious manhood beliefs are measurable across 62 nations but endorsement levels differ substantially between societies.
original_study: Bosson, Vandello et al. cross-cultural study
effect_size: Psychometric invariance across 13 regions; substantial cross-national variation
limitations: Cross-sectional; national aggregation obscures within-country variation

claim: Traditional masculinity ideology predicted about 11.4% of variance in professional psychological help-seeking attitudes among young Chinese-Indonesian men.
effect_size: 11.4% of variance
confidence: MODERATE for this sample; LOW for Indonesian men generally
limitations: Small; young; urban; ethnic-minority-specific; cross-sectional; no wording manipulation

claim: In an urban Surabaya sample, masculinity ideology, masculine norms and gender-role conflict showed NO significant correlation with primary healthcare use.
effect_size: Non-significant: p=.455, .654, .300
limitations: Cross-sectional; one urban sample; physical rather than mental health; no framing manipulation

claim: Indonesian men's health management is frequently delegated to wives; erectile dysfunction is experienced as 'losing a sense of masculinity'; overloaded Puskesmas queues and short consultations leave no room to raise sensitive concerns.
population: Men with type-2 diabetes and erectile dysfunction
predictor_iv: Masculinity; household division of labour; service design
effect_size: Not quantified
direction: Care is relational; institutions deter disclosure
limitations: Small; specific clinical population; Javanese-weighted

claim: Indonesian national survey data show marital status, employment and insurance status predict men's health-seeking; illness is widely read as takdir (fate); silence is framed by a 'macho male maxim of strength in silence'.
effect_size: Divorced young men markedly worse; self-employed/salaried seek care more than unemployed/low-income
limitations: Secondary survey data; not mental-health-specific throughout

claim: Indonesian general practitioners withheld psychiatric referrals until patients returned with self-harm injuries; 56.7% of an affected sample were unemployed and could not meet travel and out-of-pocket costs.
population: People with mental disorders (not men only)
effect_size: Not quantified for the referral finding
direction: Institutional barrier is severe and prior to any wording
limitations: Not men-only; qualitative; single-country

claim: Javanese-Islamic concepts reframe illness management as active religious duty (ngelakoni), family caretaking as ngemong, and communal ritual (slametan) reintegrates the ill; neighbours brought the ill man to hospital.
original_study: Subandi et al. first-episode psychosis case study
effect_size: Not quantified
direction: Religion and community can facilitate as well as inhibit
limitations: Single case; Javanese-Muslim; not generalisable to prevalence

claim: Across a critical interpretive synthesis of 154 studies read against 6 Indonesian studies, Community and socio-economic status are the dominant social determinants of men's health-seeking in both Global North and Global South; Religion is dramatically more prominent in the Global South.
country: 154 studies (100 Global North, 50 Global South, 4 mixed); 6 Indonesian
effect_size: Community 78.6%; SES 70.1%; Religion 5% North vs 34% South (29-point gap); Community 100% of Indonesian studies
confidence: STRONG for corpus structure; INTERPRETIVE for conclusions
limitations: Interpretive not aggregative; only 6 Indonesian studies; Javanese/Muslim-weighted; author states own positionality

claim: The 'individual help-seeker' at the centre of Global North frameworks does not transfer to Indonesia: masculinity, distress and care are organised relationally through households and communities; community operates as both care and surveillance.
predictor_iv: HIMM individual unit vs relational unit
effect_size: Re-specified HIMM: relational core; Religion and Institution added to the wheel
limitations: Interpretive; not a prevalence or causal claim; explicitly offered as open to testing

claim: Indonesian male homosociality is abundant but confiding is rare: peer research distinguishes teman nongkrong (hangout friends) from teman curhat (confidants), and men avoid emotional reliance on male peers.
original_study: Prawiro & Purbaningrum peer-group research; Hadisuyatmana et al. (2017)
effect_size: Companionship abundant; confiding rare
limitations: Qualitative; Java-weighted; small samples

claim: A casual invitation such as 'nongkrong yuk' can function as help-seeking that requires no emotional vocabulary and no exposure to communal judgement.
original_study: Menungsa-affiliated dissertation interpretation of Levant's normative male alexithymia + Indonesian peer research
research_design: Theoretical interpretation grounded in qualitative evidence
effect_size: Not quantified
direction: Relational help-seeking is invisible to Northern measures
limitations: Not empirically tested; must not be presented as a proven wording effect

claim: In a large non-representative Indonesian survey, 18% of male respondents reported accessing mental-health services in three years versus 31% of female respondents; 73% cited health professionals' communication skills as a consideration when choosing a service.
effect_size: 18% male vs 31% female; 73% cite communication quality
confidence: MODERATE for sample; LOW as national prevalence
limitations: Self-selected; 67.3% female; 75.8% Java; young-skewed; not representative

claim: Indonesian first- and second-person pronoun choice varies strongly by genre and constructs stance and relationship rather than only reference; Colloquial Jakartan Indonesian is a distinct register, not merely informal standard Indonesian.
original_study: Sujatna et al. corpus study; Sneddon
effect_size: Strong genre-dependent variation
limitations: Not male-specific; corpus genre is not conversation; Jakarta-centred

claim: Indonesian provider masculinity can be renegotiated: fathers whose wives migrated reconstructed masculine respectability from pure breadwinning toward a bundle of paid work, childcare, financial management and housework.
effect_size: Not quantified
direction: Provider identity is flexible, not fixed
limitations: Specific transnational-family population; not generalisable

claim: Indonesian tobacco advertising historically constructed masculinity through emotional control, status, adventure/modernity and traditional values.
original_study: Nichter et al. Tobacco Control analysis
effect_size: Themes identified, not quantified
limitations: Historical; does not isolate persuasive effect; does not license transfer to health communication

claim: Indonesian sports institutions (football, basketball, badminton) consistently organise emotion collectively using kita, berjuang, dukung, bersama, and process defeat with acknowledgement, apology, gratitude for effort and commitment to improve.
original_study: Indonesian sports corpus 2024-2026 (Persebaya, Timnas basket, PBSI)
effect_size: Repeated collective framing across three sports
confidence: STRONG as observed pattern; NO causal outcome
limitations: Sports audiences are not male-only; no audience-effect measurement; must not be read as male preference

claim: Indonesian TikTok discourse around #LakiLakiTidakBercerita shows male emotional openness can attract audience reactions that reassert restrictive masculinity.
effect_size: Not quantified
direction: Norm is actively enforced, not merely descriptive
limitations: Not population-level; platform-specific; not manosphere-specific

claim: Internalisation of masculine role norms correlated with self-stigma about help-seeking among Indonesian early-adult men, accounting for roughly 9.7% of variance.
effect_size: ~9.7% of variance
limitations: Non-probability online sampling; cross-sectional; sample size not reported in accessible source

claim: In donated real TikTok viewing histories, ordinary 'cultural touchpoint' male content vastly outnumbered explicitly harmful material.
original_study: Fisher et al. Masculinity Content Classification Framework
research_design: Descriptive content classification of real viewing data
effect_size: 37.74% cultural touchpoints; 4.89% masculine-status; 0.87% degrading-health
direction: Harmful tier is small but embedded in the same ecology
confidence: STRONG (for boundary framework in sampled users)
limitations: No causal outcome measurement; three Anglophone countries; 16-25 only

claim: 63% of young men regularly engaged with at least one masculinity influencer; followers were on average MORE employed, educated, higher-income and partnered than non-followers, while reporting more distress on some measures.
effect_size: 63% follow >=1; 19% vs 11% diet pills/steroids; more optimism plus more distress
confidence: MODERATE for prevalence within its own definition; WEAK for causality
limitations: Cross-sectional; selection cannot be ruled out; 'masculinity influencer' broadly defined; not equal to manosphere membership; advocacy-organisation data, not peer-reviewed

claim: Experimentally exposing men to a manfluencer framing social change as a threat to men's status increased mistrust and misogynistic attitudes, with stronger effects among younger men reporting more past rejection.
sample_size: Survey N=2,857; experiments N=597 and N=630
outcome_dv: Mistrust; dehumanisation of women; misogynistic attitudes
effect_size: Effects statistically significant but described by authors as relatively small
limitations: Fictitious vignettes; immediate attitudes only; not long-term radicalisation or behaviour; Sweden

claim: Lower acknowledgement of men's structural privilege predicted greater perceived threat from feminists, which in turn related to stronger endorsement of manosphere attitudes.
effect_size: Significant indirect pathway
limitations: Correlational; temporal ordering unresolved; direction could run either way

claim: Ofcom's qualitative study found humour, irreverence, open debate, fitness and perceived practical usefulness were the most common attractions; participants frequently consumed selectively and rejected creators' more extreme gender claims.
effect_size: Not quantified
direction: Misogyny is often not the entry hook; partial uptake is common
limitations: Cannot estimate prevalence; likely misses the most extreme users; UK only

claim: Former incels describe entry motivated by feeling like a 'loser', being alone, lacking value, and being met with validation, 'it isn't your fault' and 'you belong here'.
outcome_dv: Subjective mechanisms of entry and retention
effect_size: Not quantified
limitations: Retrospective; self-selected; not representative; not causal

claim: A looksmaxxing community of ~6 million monthly visitors displayed intense bodily scrutiny, invasive modification advice (mewing, leg-lengthening), 'masculine demoralisation' and self-harm discourse.
effect_size: Not quantified
confidence: STRONG for community content; cannot quantify reader effects
limitations: Public forum text only; no individual psychiatric outcomes measured

claim: Algorithmic audits with synthetic vulnerable-male accounts found misogynistic recommendations rose from roughly 13% to 56% of suggested videos within five days.
original_study: Regehr et al. UCL/Kent TikTok audit
confidence: MODERATE for recommender behaviour; WEAK for human psychology
limitations: Synthetic accounts cannot experience persuasion; ecological generalisability limited

claim: Manosphere community reactions systematically reward in-group identity-signalling language, consolidating group identity over time.
effect_size: In-group markers received significantly higher social rewards
confidence: MODERATE for social-reward mechanism within one forum
limitations: Observes collective platform signals, not individual internalisation; single forum

claim: Across 105 empirical studies, sexual-violence rhetoric and practice function within core manosphere communities to consolidate male-supremacist identity under victimhood narratives.
effect_size: Not pooled
confidence: STRONG for presence; INSUFFICIENT for individual perpetration base rates
limitations: Ideology/discourse is the unit; does not estimate average-consumer behaviour

claim: Shaming and ridicule messaging aimed at incels produced no positive effect, and one shaming meme increased violent fantasies relative to control.
effect_size: No positive effect; one shaming condition INCREASED violent fantasies
limitations: Specific population; single research programme; not yet widely replicated

claim: Prebunking/inoculation improves recognition of manipulation tactics but with small effects that shrink among already-committed audiences and do not reliably change behaviour.
effect_size: Small effects; attenuated for committed audiences
limitations: Recognition does not equal behaviour change

claim: Manosphere-engaged young men are often higher-income and more optimistic yet report similar loneliness to peers (55-56% vs 54% often lonely).
effect_size: 52% middle class+; 78% American dream attainable; 55-56% vs 54% often lonely; 54% vs 38% identify masculine; 72% vs 46% endorse breadwinner
limitations: Not peer-reviewed; single poll; advocacy organisation; sample size not stated

claim: A uniquely male loneliness epidemic is contested: recent systematic review and representative polling find broadly comparable loneliness rates for men and women, though men turn to others for help less.
effect_size: Pew: 16% men vs 15% women lonely most of the time; no-close-friends gap ~9% vs 8% by 2023
direction: Loneliness is not distinctively male; help-seeking is
limitations: US-weighted; measures vary; class may matter more than gender

claim: Incel samples show very high depression, anxiety, loneliness and daily suicidal thinking; extreme inceldom resembles suicidality more than terrorism.
original_study: Costello et al.; UK Commission for Countering Extremism survey
outcome_dv: Depression; anxiety; suicidality; loneliness; bullying history
effect_size: ~39% moderate-severe depression; 43% moderate-high anxiety; 37% daily suicidal thoughts; 48% high loneliness; 86% bullied
limitations: Self-selected; incels are over-represented in scholarship relative to the wider male-content ecosystem

claim: Man Box adherence is associated with higher suicidal ideation, but reported risk multipliers differ sharply across studies and must not be merged.
author_year: Promundo/Equimundo (2017); Equimundo State of American Men (2025); Hill/Heilman et al. (2020)
effect_size: Peer-reviewed OR range 1.56-2.59; separate 2025 survey reports 6.27x, and 16.3x for provider-role failure
confidence: MODERATE for direction; CONTESTED for magnitude
limitations: Different studies/years/samples/metrics; advocacy-organisation data; cross-sectional

claim: The extreme manosphere is structurally a monetisation machine: insecurity is diagnosed and a purchasable transformation is sold, with rage-bait optimised for algorithmic reach.
effect_size: Not quantified; documented case (Theroux lost most of an invested ~GBP500)
confidence: MODERATE-STRONG for structure; EMERGING for deliberate insecurity maintenance
limitations: Intentional strategy to maintain insecurity is plausible but not systematically demonstrated

claim: Indonesian male-oriented digital ecosystems are marriage-centred rather than casual-sex-centred: content organises around achieving kemapanan (established status), meeting provider expectations and vetting a prospective wife.
effect_size: Not quantified
direction: Local configuration differs from Western paradigm
confidence: MODERATE as observed pattern; NOT audience-effect evidence
limitations: Descriptive; no audience measurement; some source-quality problems in one of the two reports

claim: Indonesian provider expectations are institutionally codified, not merely cultural: marriage law designates the husband as head of family and obliges him to provide; Islamic nafaqah is a legal duty; adat requires public financial demonstrations (uang panai, seserahan).
author_year: Law No. 1/1974 Art. 31(3), 34(1); fiqh nafaqah; adat practices
effect_size: Not quantified
direction: Provider identity is legally and religiously anchored
limitations: Institutional description; does not measure psychological effect

claim: Indonesian structural conditions plausibly intensify provider strain: ~59% informal employment, female tertiary gross enrolment (35.98%) exceeding male (31.05%), and registered marriages falling 28.63% over a decade to 1,577,255 in 2023.
original_study: BPS statistics as cited in Indonesian manosphere report
effect_size: 59% informal; APK 35.98% F vs 31.05% M; marriages -28.63% over 2014-2024
confidence: MODERATE (figures reported second-hand; verify before publication)
limitations: Cited from a secondary report rather than primary BPS release; causal link to male distress is not established

claim: Indonesian male digital vocabulary is locally distinctive: bucin (from budak cinta) for 'simp', mapan / pria berkualitas for 'high-value man', melek realita for 'red-pilled', cowok lembek as the pejorative.
effect_size: Not quantified
confidence: MODERATE as description; frequency NOT quantified
limitations: No corpus frequency data; urban/Jakarta-weighted; one source report has verifiable quality problems

claim: Indonesian male-oriented content offers validation without requiring public vulnerability: it names male exhaustion while framing composure and quiet endurance as virtues.
effect_size: Illustrative creator line: 'Gue tahu lo capek... tapi gak ada yang nanya kabar lo'
direction: This is the ecosystem's most transferable communicative function
confidence: MODERATE as observed pattern; SPECULATIVE as psychological claim
limitations: No audience-effect measurement; illustrative quotations are reconstructed, not verified transcripts

claim: Indonesian religious-masculinity ecosystems (Indonesia Tanpa Pacaran, dakwah influencers, Christian Pria Sejati retreats) address the same anxieties as the secular manosphere through rule-bound processes such as ta'aruf.
effect_size: Not quantified
direction: Religion supplies certainty and structure without secular red-pill ethics
limitations: Descriptive; conservative religious masculinity should NOT be relabelled 'manosphere' without evidence of ideological link

claim: Each additional moral-emotional word is associated with roughly 13% more sharing, replicated preregistered across five research groups.
original_study: Brady et al. preregistered replication and meta-analysis
author_year: Brady et al. (2025, PNAS Nexus); Brady et al. (2017, PNAS)
sample_size: Meta-analysis 4,821,006 observations, 27 studies; direct replication 849,266 posts
research_design: Preregistered replication + meta-analysis of observational corpora
effect_size: Pooled IRR 1.13, 95% CI [1.06,1.20]; replication ~1.17
confidence: STRONG for association; MODERATE for causal interpretation
limitations: Naturalistic data cannot randomise all wording aspects; political-domain concentration

claim: Absolute moral loading increases engagement while moral DENSITY (moral words as a proportion of the message) decreases it above a saturation point; the fitted maximum in that corpus was around 0.30.
author_year: Candia et al. (2022/2026, Nature Human Behaviour)
predictor_iv: Moral word count vs moral/non-moral ratio
effect_size: Positive for loading; declining engagement above ~0.30 density
confidence: MODERATE-HIGH for non-linearity; VERY LOW as a universal 30% rule
limitations: Corpus-specific; political/fringe platforms; dictionary-based; NOT replicated in organisational, health, Indonesian or video contexts; corpus changed between preprint and publication

claim: Moral outrage predicts virality but, holding reach constant, predicts FEWER petition signatures; agency, collective identity and prosocial language show the opposite profile.
sample_size: 1,286,442 X posts linked to 24,785 Change.org petitions
effect_size: Reposts->signatures exp(b)~1.54; direct outrage->signatures ~0.98 controlling for virality
direction: Double dissociation between reach and conversion
confidence: STRONG (very large ecological dataset with real behaviour)
limitations: Observational; no randomised wording; petition topic may confound both language and success

claim: Moral appeals have a small positive average effect on intentions and behaviour; assertive (autonomy-restricting) wording reduces their effectiveness.
original_study: Xu et al. moral appeals meta-analysis
effect_size: d=.22 overall; assertiveness undermines effectiveness
confidence: STRONG for the small average; LOW for any single universal effect
limitations: Large contextual heterogeneity; mostly short-term outcomes

claim: Corporate sociopolitical activism shows small positive pooled associations with attitudes, behaviour/intentions and stock response, but NO reliable pooled association with advertising/social-media engagement.
author_year: Braga et al. (2026, Journal of Business Research)
effect_size: r=.124; r=.084; r=.182; engagement non-significant
direction: Small positive downstream; engagement is not a valid proxy
limitations: Extremely high I-squared; search ended Sept 2023; commercial rather than nonprofit weighting

claim: Consistency over time and tangible resource commitment independently predict more favourable stakeholder responses to organisational moral positioning.
effect_size: Positive multivariate moderators (~.12-.13 for resource commitment)
limitations: Coding differences; cost can also create investor risk in some conditions

claim: Concrete descriptions of internal organisational change generate stronger perceived authenticity than abstract moral positioning; a cause-congruent promise that is then unfulfilled is especially damaging.
sample_size: Four experiments across three issue contexts
predictor_iv: Abstract vs concrete internal/external activism; promise fulfilment
effect_size: Concrete internal messaging strongest; 'congruent woke washing' most damaging
direction: Specificity increases credibility; broken congruent promises are worst
limitations: Scenario-based; authenticity perception rather than long-term behaviour

claim: Publicly observable prosocial behaviour causes observers to discount the actor's virtue by inferring less principled motives.
effect_size: Motive attribution mediates most of the discounting
confidence: STRONG for interpersonal attribution; MODERATE-LOW for direct transfer to organisations
limitations: Individual actors, not corporations; US samples

claim: Visible virality metrics causally increase outrage expression, partly through greater perceived danger.
effect_size: Significant causal increase; perceived danger mediates
limitations: Twitter/X and US samples

claim: Moral framing can persuade while simultaneously moralising the attitude and reducing willingness to compromise.
effect_size: Moral frames persuaded AND moralised; reduced compromise
direction: Persuasion and depolarisation are different goals
limitations: Narrow issue set; short-term outcomes

claim: Audiences who disagree with an organisational moral stance punish it substantially more than aligned audiences reward it.
author_year: Mukherjee & Althuizen (2020, IJRM); Hydock et al. (2020)
effect_size: Opponents punish roughly twice as intensely as supporters reward
limitations: Specific contested issues; lab conditions may inflate political salience relative to habit

claim: In Indonesia, religious authority and subjective norms drove actual consumer boycott behaviour following MUI Fatwa No. 83/2023, with brand image statistically insignificant.
predictor_iv: Religious authority; subjective norms; perceived behavioural control
effect_size: Subjective norms and religious authority significant; brand image not
direction: Communal moral authority outweighs brand-level affect
limitations: Cross-sectional self-report; crisis-state geopolitical environment; not generalisable to routine communication

claim: A commercial brand campaign moralising masculinity generated enormous engagement of overwhelmingly negative valence.
original_study: Gillette 'We Believe: The Best Men Can Be'
sample_size: ~23m YouTube views; ~1.1m dislikes vs ~620k likes at one snapshot
effect_size: Dislikes exceeded likes; boycott demands; contested $8bn write-down attribution
direction: Backfire for moral scolding by a commercial source
confidence: MODERATE as a case; NOT a controlled test
limitations: Confounded by market shifts to DTC razors, creative execution, historical moment; engagement is not approval
